techniques.name: Model Cards
techniques.description: Model cards are standardised documentation frameworks that systematically document machine learning models through structured templates. The templates cover intended use cases, performance metrics across different demographic groups and operating conditions, training data characteristics, evaluation procedures, limitations, and ethical considerations. They serve as comprehensive technical specifications that enable informed model selection, prevent inappropriate deployment, support regulatory compliance, and facilitate fair assessment by providing transparent reporting of model capabilities and constraints across diverse populations and scenarios.

example_use_cases.description: Documenting a medical diagnosis AI with detailed performance metrics across different patient demographics, age groups, and clinical conditions, enabling healthcare providers to understand when the model should be trusted and when additional expert consultation is needed for patient safety.

Creating comprehensive model cards for hiring algorithms that transparently report performance differences across demographic groups, helping HR departments identify potential bias issues and ensure equitable candidate evaluation processes.

Publishing detailed model documentation for a credit scoring API that clearly describes training data sources, evaluation methodologies, and performance limitations, enabling financial institutions to make informed decisions about model deployment and regulatory compliance.

limitations.description: Creating comprehensive model cards requires substantial time, expertise, and resources to gather performance data across diverse conditions and demographic groups, potentially delaying model deployment timelines.
Information can become outdated quickly as models are retrained, updated, or deployed in new contexts, requiring ongoing maintenance and version control to remain accurate and useful.
Organisations may provide incomplete or superficial documentation to avoid revealing competitive advantages or potential liabilities, undermining the transparency goals of model cards.
Lack of standardised formats and enforcement mechanisms means model card quality and completeness vary significantly across different organisations and use cases.
Technical complexity of documenting model behaviour across all relevant dimensions may exceed the expertise of some development teams, leading to gaps in critical information.

resources.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
resources.abstract: Trained machine learning models are increasingly used to perform high-impact tasks in areas such as law enforcement, medicine, education, and employment. In order to clarify the intended use cases of machine learning models and minimize their usage in contexts for which they are not well suited, we recommend that released models be accompanied by documentation detailing their performance characteristics. In this paper, we propose a framework that we call model cards, to encourage such transparent model reporting. Model cards are short documents accompanying trained machine learning models that provide benchmarked evaluation in a variety of conditions, such as across different cultural, demographic, or phenotypic groups (e.g., race, geographic location, sex, Fitzpatrick skin type) and intersectional groups (e.g., age and race, or sex and Fitzpatrick skin type) that are relevant to the intended application domains. Model cards also disclose the context in which models are intended to be used, details of the performance evaluation procedures, and other relevant information. While we focus primarily on human-centered machine learning models in the application fields of computer vision and natural language processing, this framework can be used to document any trained machine learning model. To solidify the concept, we provide cards for two supervised models: One trained to detect smiling faces in images, and one trained to detect toxic comments in text. We propose model cards as a step towards the responsible democratization of machine learning and related AI technology, increasing transparency into how well AI technology works. We hope this work encourages those releasing trained machine learning models to accompany model releases with similar detailed evaluation numbers and other relevant documentation.

resources.title: Systematic analysis of 32,111 AI model cards characterizes documentation practice in AI
Interactive Model Cards: A Human-Centered Approach to Model Documentation
resources.abstract: Deep learning models for natural language processing (NLP) are increasingly adopted and deployed by analysts without formal training in NLP or machine learning (ML). However, the documentation intended to convey the model’s details and appropriate use is tailored primarily to individuals with ML or NLP expertise. To address this gap, we conduct a design inquiry into interactive model cards, which augment traditionally static model cards with affordances for exploring model documentation and interacting with the models themselves. Our investigation consists of an initial conceptual study with experts in ML, NLP, and AI Ethics, followed by a separate evaluative study with non-expert analysts who use ML models in their work. Using a semi-structured interview format coupled with a think-aloud protocol, we collected feedback from a total of 30 participants who engaged with different versions of standard and interactive model cards. Through a thematic analysis of the collected data, we identified several conceptual dimensions that summarize the strengths and limitations of standard and interactive model cards, including: stakeholders; design; guidance; understandability & interpretability; sensemaking & skepticism; and trust & safety. Our findings demonstrate the importance of carefully considered design and interactivity for orienting and supporting non-expert analysts using deep learning models, along with a need for consideration of broader sociotechnical contexts and organizational dynamics. We have also identified design elements, such as language, visual cues, and warnings, among others, that support interactivity and make non-interactive content accessible. We summarize our findings as design guidelines and discuss their implications for a human-centered approach towards AI/ML documentation.

sample_claims.text: The model's performance characteristics are documented across all relevant demographic groups and operating conditions
The diagnostic system's accuracy and error rates are reported separately for each patient subpopulation
The model's intended use cases and known limitations are clearly communicated to decision-makers
The lending model's approval rates and error distributions are transparently reported for all applicant demographics
The system's training data characteristics, evaluation procedures, and ethical considerations are comprehensively documented

techniques.name: Datasheets for Datasets
techniques.description: Datasheets for datasets establish comprehensive documentation standards for datasets, systematically recording creation methodology, data composition, collection procedures, preprocessing transformations, intended applications, potential biases, privacy considerations, and maintenance protocols. These structured documents enhance dataset transparency by providing essential context for appropriate usage, enabling informed decisions about dataset suitability for specific tasks, supporting bias detection and mitigation efforts, ensuring compliance with data protection regulations, and promoting responsible data stewardship throughout the entire data lifecycle from collection to disposal.

example_use_cases.description: Documenting a medical imaging dataset with detailed information about patient privacy protections, anonymisation procedures, and data sharing constraints to ensure sensitive health information is handled appropriately and regulatory compliance is maintained.

Creating comprehensive datasheets for recruitment datasets that document demographic representation across different job categories, helping developers identify potential bias in training data and develop more equitable hiring algorithms.

Establishing transparent documentation for financial transaction datasets that clearly describes data collection methodology, preprocessing steps, and intended use cases, enabling researchers to make informed decisions about dataset appropriateness for their specific applications.

Documenting a safety-critical autonomous vehicle perception dataset with records of sensor calibration procedures, environmental conditions during collection, edge-case scenario coverage, and known distributional gaps, enabling safety engineers to assess whether training data adequately represents the operating conditions required for safe deployment and to support regulatory type-approval submissions.

Documenting the statistical distributions, temporal coverage, and known quality characteristics of training datasets to support model monitoring pipelines, enabling operations teams to detect data drift and assess whether production data remains within the documented training distribution for informed decisions about model retraining or recalibration.

limitations.description: Creating thorough datasheets requires significant time investment and domain expertise to properly document collection methods, biases, and ethical considerations, potentially delaying dataset release or publication.
Information may become outdated as datasets undergo preprocessing, cleaning, or augmentation, requiring ongoing maintenance to ensure documentation accuracy throughout the data lifecycle.
Absence of standardised templates and enforcement mechanisms leads to inconsistent documentation quality and completeness across different organisations and research communities.
Dataset creators may intentionally omit sensitive information about collection methods, participant consent, or potential biases to avoid legal liability or competitive disadvantage.
Limited adoption and awareness means many existing datasets lack proper documentation, creating gaps in the historical record and making legacy dataset assessment difficult.

resources.title: Datasheets for Datasets
resources.abstract: The machine learning community currently has no standardized process for documenting datasets, which can lead to severe consequences in high-stakes domains. To address this gap, we propose datasheets for datasets. In the electronics industry, every component, no matter how simple or complex, is accompanied with a datasheet that describes its operating characteristics, test results, recommended uses, and other information. By analogy, we propose that every dataset be accompanied with a datasheet that documents its motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and so on. Datasheets for datasets will facilitate better communication between dataset creators and dataset consumers, and encourage the machine learning community to prioritize transparency and accountability.

resources.title: Understanding Machine Learning Practitioners' Data Documentation Perceptions, Needs, Challenges, and Desiderata
resources.abstract: Data is central to the development and evaluation of machine learning (ML) models. However, the use of problematic or inappropriate datasets can result in harms when the resulting models are deployed. To encourage responsible AI practice through more deliberate reflection on datasets and transparency around the processes by which they are created, researchers and practitioners have begun to advocate for increased data documentation and have proposed several data documentation frameworks. However, there is little research on whether these data documentation frameworks meet the needs of ML practitioners, who both create and consume datasets. To address this gap, we set out to understand ML practitioners' data documentation perceptions, needs, challenges, and desiderata, with the goal of deriving design requirements that can inform future data documentation frameworks. We conducted a series of semi-structured interviews with 14 ML practitioners at a single large, international technology company. We had them answer a list of questions taken from datasheets for datasets (Gebru, 2021). Our findings show that current approaches to data documentation are largely ad hoc and myopic in nature. Participants expressed needs for data documentation frameworks to be adaptable to their contexts, integrated into their existing tools and workflows, and automated wherever possible. Despite the fact that data documentation frameworks are often motivated from the perspective of responsible AI, participants did not make the connection between the questions that they were asked to answer and their responsible AI implications. In addition, participants often had difficulties prioritizing the needs of dataset consumers and providing information that someone unfamiliar with their datasets might need to know. Based on these findings, we derive seven design requirements for future data documentation frameworks.

resources.title: Datasheets for Datasets help ML Engineers Notice and Understand Ethical Issues in Training Data
resources.abstract: The social computing community has demonstrated interest in the ethical issues sometimes produced by machine learning (ML) models, like violations of privacy, fairness, and accountability. This paper discovers what kinds of ethical considerations machine learning engineers recognize, how they build understanding, and what decisions they make when working with a real-world dataset. In particular, it illustrates ways in which Datasheets for Datasets, an accountability intervention designed to help engineers explore unfamiliar training data, scaffolds the process of issue discovery, understanding, and ethical decision-making. Participants were asked to review an intentionally ethically problematic dataset and asked to think aloud as they used it to solve a given ML problem. Out of 23 participants, 11 were given a Datasheet they could use while completing the task. Participants were ethically sensitive enough to identify concerns in the dataset; participants who had a Datasheet did open and refer to it; and those with Datasheets mentioned ethical issues during the think-aloud earlier and more often than than those without. The think-aloud protocol offered a grounded description of how participants recognized, understood, and made a decision about ethical problems in an unfamiliar dataset. The method used in this study can test other interventions that claim to encourage recognition, promote understanding, and support decision-making among technologists.

sample_claims.text: The training dataset's collection methodology, participant consent procedures, and intended use constraints are documented and accessible to model developers
The dataset composition across demographic groups and protected characteristics is documented to enable bias detection during model development
The dataset's privacy protections, anonymisation procedures, and re-identification risks are documented before data sharing
The data provenance from original sources through preprocessing transformations is traceable for regulatory review
The environmental sensing dataset documents geographic coverage, temporal distribution, and known measurement biases across different operating conditions

techniques.name: CycloneDX Machine Learning Bill of Materials
techniques.description: A CycloneDX ML-BOM (machine-learning bill of materials) is a machine-readable inventory of what a model is made of, written in the CycloneDX standard (ECMA-424) so that tools as well as people can check it. It applies the software bill of materials, a structured list of the components in a piece of software, to models: the model is declared as a component of type machine-learning-model with its identifiers, version, supplier, licence and file hashes, together with the base models it was derived from (its pedigree), the datasets used to train and evaluate it with their source, classification and owners, the libraries it depends on, and an optional structured model card giving its task, architecture, performance metrics, intended uses and known limitations. The BOM is written at release, by hand or with a generator that reads the model's repository and metadata, checked against the CycloneDX schema, and can be signed. Consumers then query it, for example to find every deployed model that uses a dataset or library found to be compromised, or to check a supplier's declared datasets and licences before purchase. Unlike a model card or datasheet, written for people to read, or an experiment log or data version history, which stay with the team that built the model, it is a parts list in a fixed schema that travels with the model and can be matched against vulnerability records and file hashes, but it records what its author declares and verifies none of it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank keeps an ML-BOM for every deployed model, recording each base model by its Hugging Face package URL and revision, the fine-tuning datasets, the framework libraries and the file hashes. When a compromised base-model release or a vulnerability in a model-loading library is announced, its security team queries the BOMs to list the affected deployments within hours and decides which to withdraw or patch.

A hospital trust buying a diagnostic imaging model requires the supplier to deliver a signed ML-BOM with each version. Before the model enters clinical evaluation, the acceptance team checks the BOM's signature, compares its file hashes with the delivered files and checks the listed libraries against known-vulnerability records.

A government department procuring a document-classification model asks bidders for an ML-BOM whose model-card and dataset fields declare each training and evaluation dataset with its source, licence and owner, and the model's known technical limitations. Its assessors and later its auditors read and query these declarations to compare bids and to check what the chosen supplier said it used.

A software company generates an ML-BOM for each release of its customer-support assistant with an open-source generator, recording the base and embedding models, the quantised model file and the framework libraries with hashes. Its security team compares each new BOM with the previous release's to catch an unreviewed change of base model or library before the release ships.

limitations.description: It records what its author declares. Nothing in the format checks that the listed datasets were the ones used, that the model-card fields are true or that the list is complete, so a BOM is evidence that a disclosure was made, not that it is accurate. Hashes and a signature show that the document and the files it lists have not changed since it was written, which is a different thing.

Almost every field is optional: ECMA-424 requires a component's type and name and little else, so a BOM can pass schema validation while saying almost nothing. In a 2026 preprint that generated ML-BOMs with one open-source tool for about 98,000 Hugging Face models, every BOM had the required fields, but only 39% named a dataset, 17% listed technical limitations and 0.2% had a meaningful description. A claim needs the fields it relies on to be checked, not only schema validity.

Generators can fill only what they can read: hub metadata, model-card text and configuration files. Training data, fine-tuning history and settings that the publisher never wrote down stay empty, and for a model bought from a supplier the BOM is only as complete as the supplier chooses to make it.

Each BOM describes one version of one model. Fine-tuning, quantisation, a new framework release or a changed dataset needs a new BOM, and the ability to answer 'which of our models use this component?' when a compromise is disclosed depends on BOMs being regenerated and kept for every deployed version, which is a standing process cost rather than a one-off task.

techniques.name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
techniques.description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's model risk team logs every complaint from customers or staff about its credit, fraud and customer-chatbot models that meets the OECD definition of an AI incident or hazard. A wrongly refused loan, an account frozen by a fraud alert and a chatbot quoting the wrong fees are recorded on the same severity scale and harm types, with the model and version and how the model was involved, so the quarterly risk committee can see which systems recur and which harms dominate.

A hospital records near misses as well as harms. When a radiologist notices that the imaging triage model has put an urgent scan at the back of the queue, the event is logged as an AI hazard, with the model's erroneous ranking as a direct cause, its autonomy recorded as human-in-the-loop, and the action taken, so that patterns of near misses are visible before one becomes an incident.

A national regulator that receives AI incident reports from deployers in several sectors asks for them in the OECD format, with a published note on how it judges seriousness, so that it can count serious incidents by sector and harm type and compare its figures with those of other authorities using the same fields.

A city transport authority running an AI traffic-signal optimiser records a period of emergency-vehicle delays as an incident affecting critical infrastructure, with the system as a contributing factor and an operator's configuration change as human error, so the record shows both causes and the follow-up actions assigned to the supplier and to its own staff.

limitations.description: A register is only as complete as the reports that reach it. Harms nobody notices, such as people quietly refused a service, and events staff have reasons not to report go unrecorded, so a short register is weak evidence that a system has caused little harm unless the organisation can also show how incidents are detected and how reporting is encouraged.

The OECD's own definitions say that seriousness is highly context-dependent, that each jurisdiction may define it differently, and that several small incidents can add up to a serious one. Two reporters can classify the same event differently, so counts of serious incidents can be compared only between reporters that share a written severity rule.

The framework standardises what is recorded, not how an incident is investigated or fixed, and the OECD paper explicitly gives no guidance on corrective or preventive action. Its field for how the AI system was involved is a short category list, and the fields on training data and the model are optional free text, so an organisation needs its own root-cause and follow-up process if records are to lead to changes.

None of the seven mandatory fields identifies the system or its version, the organisation that deployed it or the date of the event. Records kept to the mandatory minimum cannot trace incidents to a model release or show repeated failures of one system; the framework lets a reporting scheme make more fields mandatory, and an organisation that needs this traceability has to do so.

The framework is a recent proposal that the OECD planned to test through open submissions to its AI Incidents Monitor. Regulators that impose a legal duty to report incidents set their own format, categories and deadlines, so an organisation under such a duty reports in the regulator's format, may need to keep the OECD fields alongside, and cannot assume that an event serious on the OECD scale meets the legal definition of a serious incident, or the reverse.

sample_claims.text: Every incident and near miss reported for the imaging triage model since deployment is recorded with all seven mandatory OECD fields completed and its severity assigned under the hospital's written severity rule.
Each incident recorded for the bank's credit and fraud models identifies the model and version involved and how the AI system contributed, so repeated failures of one release can be traced.
Every incident recorded as serious in the register has at least one action taken recorded against it (prevention, mitigation, ceasing or remediation), with a description of what was done.

Each incident recorded for the traffic-signal optimiser lists every way the system was involved, including human error where an operator's action contributed, so that the causes attributable to the supplier and to the operator can be traced.

techniques.name: AI FactSheets
techniques.description: AI FactSheets is a documentation practice in which the developer or supplier of an AI model or service answers a structured set of questions about it, modelled on the supplier's declarations of conformity that industries such as telecommunications and transport use to give written assurance, with evidence, that a product meets stated requirements. The questions cover the service's purpose and its intended and unsuitable uses, the datasets it was trained and tested on, its test methods and results (reported for groups such as age bands or genders where relevant), checks for bias, explainability, behaviour on data unlike its training data and robustness to adversarial attack, how user data is secured, and its lineage, such as when and how its models were retrained; 'N/A' and 'Proprietary' are allowed answers. Facts are gathered from the people in each role across the lifecycle (business owner, data scientist, model validator and operations engineer), and any change to the service produces a new version of the FactSheet while earlier versions are kept. The originating group's seven-step method designs the template with its readers: interview the people who will read the facts and those who will produce them, draft and trial a template of questions, have the real producers complete it, evaluate the result with its readers for content and presentation, and build further templates for other audiences such as a review board or regulator. Unlike a model card, which reports one model's intended use and evaluation to the people choosing it, or a datasheet, which describes one dataset, a FactSheet may cover one model or a whole service built from several models and datasets (attaching their datasheets), gathers facts from each role in the lifecycle and has a different template for each audience; unlike a CycloneDX ML-BOM it is written for people to read rather than as a machine-readable parts list for software tools.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital trust buying a speech-to-text service for clinical dictation sends bidders a FactSheet template asking for intended and unsuitable uses, training data, retraining frequency, behaviour on noisy audio, and word error rates by speaker accent and age band on recordings the trust supplies. The panel compares the answers to shortlist bidders, re-tests the shortlisted services on its own recordings, and writes the confirmed error rates into the contract as service levels.

A bank's model risk team follows the seven-step method to design a FactSheet template for credit models: it interviews validators about the decisions they make and data scientists about the facts they can record, then has the scientists complete it for a new affordability model. Validators read the completed FactSheet's training data, performance, bias checks and known weak cases before deciding whether to approve the model for deployment.

A company selling a sentiment-analysis API publishes a short FactSheet for developers browsing its catalogue, giving the purpose, input and output formats, training data, accuracy and the kinds of text the service handles poorly. From the same facts it generates a longer FactSheet, with a different template, for enterprise customers' risk and compliance reviewers.

A city council's AI ethics review board asks each supplier for a FactSheet in a template written for the board, covering training and test data distributions, data handling, the inputs the service handles poorly and possible sources of unfair outcomes. The board reads them before deciding whether a photo-based street-repair reporting service may go live.

limitations.description: A FactSheet is the supplier's own declaration. As with the declarations of conformity it imitates, the supplier runs the tests it reports and nothing in the format checks them, so it shows what was claimed rather than that the claims hold. A buyer who relies on a declared figure has to re-test the service or ask for third-party testing, which the original proposal expects only for the highest-stakes, regulated, enterprise and public-sector applications.

Facts not recorded while the service is built are hard to recover. In IBM's own trials, developers forgot how they had transformed training data or which settings they had tried, and recovering the training-data transformations for one FactSheet took several hours over two days although the dataset was small and its author was available. A FactSheet written after development is likely to have gaps or errors unless fact collection is part of the development process.

The format accepts 'N/A' and 'Proprietary' as answers. In IBM's trials most developers assumed bias would not be an issue and marked bias questions not applicable, even where further questioning showed it could be, and participants were unsure how much detail they could give without losing competitive advantage. An unchallenged 'N/A' can hide a risk nobody examined, and items withheld as proprietary are often the ones a buyer would need in order to check the self-declared results.

There is no single FactSheet. Its authors hold that one template cannot serve every audience and domain, and developers report the metrics conventional for their kind of model, so FactSheets from different suppliers often cannot be compared unless the buyer fixes the questions, metrics and test conditions in its own template.

Whether readers understand FactSheets and decide better with them is untested. Producers in IBM's studies found it hard to know what readers needed and often left out what a less expert reader would need. The design method checks a draft with a few intended readers, and the group's later case studies report that producers could follow it, but none of these sources tests whether buyers, validators or review boards read FactSheets correctly or make better decisions with them.

resources.title: ibm-aigov-facts-client
A Methodology for Creating AI FactSheets
resources.abstract: As AI models and services are used in a growing number of highstakes areas, a consensus is forming around the need for a clearer record of how these models and services are developed to increase trust. Several proposals for higher quality and more consistent AI documentation have emerged to address ethical and legal concerns and general social impacts of such systems. However, there is little published work on how to create this documentation. This is the first work to describe a methodology for creating the form of AI documentation we call FactSheets. We have used this methodology to create useful FactSheets for nearly two dozen models. This paper describes this methodology and shares the insights we have gathered. Within each step of the methodology, we describe the issues to consider and the questions to explore with the relevant people in an organization who will be creating and consuming the AI facts in a FactSheet. This methodology will accelerate the broader adoption of transparent AI documentation.

FactSheets for Hardware-Aware AI Models: A Case Study of Analog In Memory Computing AI Models

sample_claims.text: The supplier's FactSheet for the dictation service states its intended and unsuitable uses, the datasets it was tested on, and its word error rate on each, reported separately by speaker accent and age band.

Each production version of the affordability model has a FactSheet to which its data scientist and validator contributed before deployment and its operations engineer after, and the FactSheets of earlier versions are retained unchanged.
Every FactSheet item a supplier answered 'N/A' or 'Proprietary' carries a stated reason, and the review board accepted each reason before approving the service.
The FactSheet template used to assess suppliers was evaluated with the procurement and risk assessors who read it before first use, and the items they found missing or unclear were revised.

techniques.name: UK Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard Record
techniques.description: An Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) record is a public account that a UK public sector organisation writes about one algorithmic tool it uses, on the UK government's standard template, and publishes in a central repository on GOV.UK. The template has two tiers: a short plain-language summary for the general public (what the tool is, why it is used and a contact), and eight further sheets for specialist readers such as journalists, researchers and civil society, covering who is accountable for the tool and which suppliers were involved, how it works and what it replaced, how its output feeds into decisions, when a person reviews that output, how members of the public can appeal, the system's and each model's inputs, outputs, architecture and performance (including any bias testing), the data used, and the impact assessments, risks and mitigations. Information that would be exempt under the Freedom of Information Act can be left out or summarised field by field, with the reason stated, and the record is cleared by the tool's team, its senior responsible owner (the role accountable for the tool) and the press office, checked for readability by the central ATRS team, and updated when the tool changes substantially or is retired. Publishing is mandatory for central government departments and for arm's-length bodies that deliver public or frontline services or deal directly with the public, for tools in beta, pilot or production that significantly influence decisions affecting the public or interact with it directly; other public bodies may publish voluntarily. Unlike a model card, written by a developer for people choosing a model, or a supplier's AI FactSheet for buyers, an ATRS record is written by the deploying public body for the public and describes the decision process, human review and appeal routes around the tool as well as the tool.

example_use_cases.description: A government department piloting a machine-learning model that prioritises benefit claims for caseworker checks publishes an ATRS record before the pilot starts. It tells claimants, journalists and MPs that the score only orders the caseworkers' queue and a caseworker makes every decision, how claimants can ask for a review, what kinds of data the model uses and what bias testing was done.

A district council piloting a supplier's tool that ranks rent-arrears cases for housing officers publishes a voluntary ATRS record. Because the record needs the model type, a description of the training data and performance figures, the council's procurement team writes their supply into the contract, and the record names the supplier, its role and the terms of its access to tenants' data.

A police force using a domestic-abuse risk assessment tool publishes a voluntary record in which the fields that would show how to evade the tool are marked exempt, with the reason, while the summary, the officers' review of each score, the appeal route and the risk mitigations are published in full for oversight bodies and community groups to examine.

A department launching a chatbot that answers questions about a public service publishes a record because the tool interacts directly with the public. The record states that answers come from a named provider's large language model used as supplied, how answers are checked, how often conversations are reviewed and how a user reaches a human adviser.

limitations.description: A record is the deploying body's own account. The central ATRS team checks drafts for readability, not accuracy, and nothing in the standard tests the stated performance, bias testing or human review against the tool's behaviour. A record is also only as current as its last update, which depends on the body resubmitting after a substantial change, so it shows what was disclosed and when, not that the tool works as described.

The mandatory scope is narrow: central government departments and qualifying arm's-length bodies, and only tools that significantly influence decisions with public effect or interact directly with the public, from the beta or pilot stage on. Local authorities, police forces and other bodies outside central government publish voluntarily, and analytical models that inform policy are usually out of scope, so the absence of a record does not show that no tool is in use.

Fields can be withheld or summarised under Freedom of Information exemptions, including commercial interests, and no record is published where even the tool's existence cannot be confirmed. Police and commercial interviewees in a 2022 study expected suppliers to resist disclosing proprietary details, so the technical tier of a record for a procured tool can be thin unless the contract requires the supplier to provide the information.

For an off-the-shelf model that the organisation has not trained, tested or refined, such as a large language model used through its web interface, the guidance says to leave the model and development data sections blank. Records for such tools say nothing about the model's training data or evaluation, which is often what a reader most needs in order to judge them.

Whether the public can find, understand and use records has not been tested. Records sit in a repository on GOV.UK rather than reaching people when a decision affects them, although the 2021 public engagement study behind the two-tier design found people wanted active notice for higher-impact uses. Police interviewees in a 2022 study feared records would give more detail than the public needs and accuracy figures without context; its authors called for evaluation with impacted communities.

sample_claims.text: An ATRS record for the claim-prioritisation model was published on GOV.UK before the pilot began, stating the model's role in decisions, when a caseworker reviews its output and how claimants can ask for a review.
Every algorithmic tool in the department's inventory that falls within the ATRS mandatory scope and is in beta, pilot or production has a published ATRS record.

Each field withheld from the published record is marked exempt with its reason, and each exemption was cleared by the tool's senior responsible owner, under the ATRS scope and exemptions policy, before publication.
The published ATRS record was updated within one month of the model being retrained on new data or its role in the decision process changing.
